unit.unitOverview: Say what you have done and what you have not done yet. Use have and has with the past form: I have posted it. Put yet, already and still in the right place. Start a sentence with the time part: Before I leave, I check the list.
unit.learningPath:
The lesson: listen, then say each line.
Words: 28 words for errands, forms and time.
Patterns: 3 cards. Read the worked one first.
Reading: two short texts and a counter notice.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, then listen back.
Writing: four tasks. Made-up answers are fine.
Practice: six exercises. Check each one with the answers.
Quiz: 12 questions. Then look at My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
Hello. This is Unit 3.
In this unit you say what you have done.
You also say what you have not done yet.
Think of one day of errands.
A form to fill in. A letter to post. A box to collect.
Listen to this sentence.
I have posted the letter.
Have, then posted. Two words, one idea.
It means: the letter is gone. That part is finished.
You do not say when. The day is not the point.
The point is how things stand now.
With he, she and it, use has.
She has signed the form. He has paid for it.
With I, you, we and they, use have.
Many verbs take -ed after have.
Post, posted. Fill, filled. Collect, collected. Print, printed.
Some verbs change. Send, sent. Take, taken. Give, given. Do, done. Get, got.
For a place, say been. I have been to the post office.
Now the small words for time.
Yet goes at the end, and only when a thing is not done.
I have not sent it yet.
Have you sent it yet?
Already goes in the middle, before the past form.
I have already sent it.
Already means: sooner than you thought.
Still goes in front of have not.
I still have not sent it.
Still means: nothing has changed, and now it is late.
Just means a very short time ago.
I have just come back from the counter.
Recently and lately go at the end.
I have not been to that office lately.
Here is one rule to hold on to.
With a time word like yesterday, use the past.
I posted it yesterday. Not: I have posted it yesterday.
Now the last pattern.
Two parts in one sentence. One part says when.
Before I leave, I check the list.
The when part comes first. Then a comma. Then the main part.
After I fill in the form, I sign it.
When the queue is long, I come back later.
You can turn it round. I check the list before I leave.
Then you need no comma.
That is the whole unit.
Have and has for a finished thing, with no day said.
Yet, already and still in their own places.
And the time part first, with a comma.
Now do the three cards, then the practice.
Say every line out loud. Your voice is part of the lesson.

readings.title: Three things done, two things left
readings.setting: One o'clock, in the middle of a day of errands.
readings.passageScript:
It is one o'clock, and I have done three things on my list.
I have posted the two letters. The envelopes are gone.
I have collected the box from the shop on the corner.
And I have just come back from the bank.
The queue there was long, but it was quick.
Two things are still on the list.
I have not renewed my library card yet. The library closes at five.
I have not filled in the application for the English course yet.
It needs my signature and one document with my address.
I have already printed the form, so that part is done.
Before I go out again, I check the list.
After I renew the card, I will fill in the application at home.
I have not been to the post office lately, so I had no stamps.
Now I have ten.

readings.title: Before you go to the office
readings.setting: Advice about an appointment at a public office.
readings.passageScript:
An appointment is an hour that is yours. Here is what people do.
Before you leave home, you check three things.
First, the date and the hour of the appointment.
Second, your reference. It is the short number on your letter.
Third, your documents. Most offices want one with your name and your address.
Print the form at home if you can.
Fill in every line. An empty line sends the form back to you.
Sign at the end. A form with no signature is not finished.
When you arrive, stand in the queue for the counter.
The worker checks the form and stamps it.
Ask for a receipt before you leave, and keep it.
If you cannot come, cancel the appointment. Do not just stay at home.
Offices give the hour to another person, and you get a new date.
Many people have waited weeks for nothing, because they forgot this.

grammar.title: Posted, sent, collected: finished, with no date
grammar.explanation:
Use have or has with the past form when a thing is finished now.
You do not say when it happened.
I have posted the letter. The letter is gone.
With he, she and it, use has: She has signed it.
With a time word like yesterday, use the past: I posted it yesterday.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I have posted the letter.
You have filled in the form.
We have collected the card.
They have cancelled it.

He has signed it.
She has printed a copy.
It has arrived.

Not done:
I have not posted it.
She has not signed it.

Ask:
Have you posted it?
Yes, I have. No, I have not.

The form after have or has:
post: posted
fill: filled
cancel: cancelled
send: sent
take: taken
give: given
do: done
get: got
go to a place: been
grammar.workedExample:
She ___ ___ the form. (sign)
1. The person is she, so use has.
2. Sign takes -ed: sign, signed.
3. After has, put signed.
4. She has signed the form.
5. Check: has, then one past form? Yes.
6. Check: no time word like yesterday? Yes. Good.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to keep the past form on its own after have.
No: I have sent it yesterday.
Yes: I sent it yesterday. The day is said, so use the past.
Yes: I have sent it. No day is said.
No: She have signed it.
Yes: She has signed it.
grammar.memoryTip: A day in the sentence? Use the past. No day? Use have or has.
grammar.practice:
Write have or has, and the right form of the word.
1. I ___ ___ the two letters. (post)
2. She ___ ___ the application. (submit)
3. We ___ ___ the box from the shop. (collect)
4. He ___ ___ his card. (renew)
5. They ___ not ___ the form yet. (stamp)
6. ___ you ___ the document? (print)
7. The letter ___ ___ this morning. (arrive)
8. I ___ ___ my name at the end. (sign)
grammar.answerKey:
1. have posted  2. has submitted  3. have collected  4. has renewed  5. have, stamped  6. Have, printed  7. has arrived  8. have signed
Has goes with he, she, it and the letter. Have goes with I, you, we and they.
Wrong on 7? The letter is one thing, so it takes has.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read the card again and do it twice.

grammar.title: Yet at the end, already in the middle
grammar.explanation:
Yet goes at the end, and only when a thing is not done.
I have not filled in the form yet.
Already goes in the middle: I have already filled it in.
Still goes in front of have not: I still have not filled it in.
Just goes in the middle too: I have just filled it in.
Recently and lately go at the end.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Not done, and you are waiting:
I have not posted it yet.
Have you posted it yet?

Done, and sooner than you thought:
I have already posted it.
She has already signed it.

Not done, and now it is late:
I still have not posted it.
The card is still at the counter.

A very short time ago:
I have just posted it.

In the last days or weeks:
I have been ill recently.
The queue has been long lately.

Where each one sits:
yet: at the end
already and just: after have or has
still: in front of have not
recently and lately: at the end
grammar.workedExample:
Put already into this sentence: I have signed the form.
1. Already goes in the middle.
2. Find have or has. Here it is have.
3. Find the past form. Here it is signed.
4. Put already between the two.
5. I have already signed the form.
6. Check: already sits between have and signed? Yes. Good.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to put yet in a sentence that is finished.
No: I have posted it yet.
Yes: I have already posted it.
Yes: I have not posted it yet.
Yet belongs in a not sentence, or in a question.

grammar.title: Before I leave, I check the list: two parts, one comma
grammar.explanation:
Two parts in one sentence. One part says when.
Put the when part first, then a comma, then the main part.
Before I leave, I check the list.
After I sign the form, I put it in the envelope.
When the queue is long, I come back later.
You can turn it round, and then there is no comma.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Time part first, with a comma:
Before I leave, I check the list.
After I fill in the form, I sign it.
When the office closes, the queue goes.

The same sentences, turned round, with no comma:
I check the list before I leave.
I sign the form after I fill it in.
The queue goes when the office closes.

The three words:
before: this part happens later
after: this part happens first
when: at that time

Both parts need a person and a verb:
Before I leave, I check the list.
Before the office closes, I post it.
grammar.workedExample:
Join these two: I check the list. I leave. (before)
1. Which part says when? I leave.
2. Put before in front of it: Before I leave.
3. That part comes first, then a comma.
4. Then the main part: I check the list.
5. Before I leave, I check the list.
6. Check: a comma after the first part? Yes.
7. Check: a capital letter at the start, a full stop at the end? Yes.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to forget the comma when the time part comes first.
No: Before I leave I check the list.
Yes: Before I leave, I check the list.
Turn it round and the comma goes:
Yes: I check the list before I leave.
grammar.memoryTip: Time part first? Put a comma after it. Time part last? No comma.

6. I stand in the queue. The office opens. (when)
7. I make a copy. I submit the application. (before)
8. I go home. The worker stamps my form. (after)

1. Before I leave, I check the list.
2. After I fill it in, I sign the form.
3. When the queue is long, I come back later.
4. After I print the form, I put it in an envelope.
5. Before I go there, I phone the office.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. have posted  2. has submitted  3. have collected  4. has renewed  5. have, stamped  6. Have, printed  7. has arrived  8. have signed
Has goes with he, she, it and the letter. Have goes with I, you, we and they.
Wrong on 7? The letter is one thing, so it takes has.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read the card again and do it twice.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. I have not renewed my card yet.
2. She has already collected the box.
3. I still have not received an answer.
4. They have just delivered the envelope.
5. Have you signed it yet?
6. The queue has been long lately.
7. He has not filled in the last page yet.
8. I have already been to the counter twice.
Wrong on 3? Still comes in front of have not, not after it.
Wrong on 2, 4 or 8? Already and just sit between have or has and the past form.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read the card again and do it twice.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. Before I leave, I check the list.
2. After I fill it in, I sign the form.
3. When the queue is long, I come back later.
4. After I print the form, I put it in an envelope.
5. Before I go there, I phone the office.
6. When the office opens, I stand in the queue.
7. Before I submit the application, I make a copy.
8. After the worker stamps my form, I go home.
No comma after the first part? That is the one thing to put right.
Wrong on 2 or 4? After marks the part that happens first.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read the card again and do it twice.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. has cancelled  2. have kept  3. have delivered  4. have printed  5. has left  6. has stamped  7. have received  8. have taken
Has goes with he, she, it and the worker. Have goes with I, you, we and they.
Wrong on 2, 5 or 8? Keep, leave and take change: kept, left, taken.
7 or 8 right: good. 5 or 6: do it again tomorrow. 4 or less: read Card 1 again first.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1 b, 2 a, 3 a, 4 b, 5 a, 6 b, 7 a, 8 b, 9 a, 10 b
Yet and lately sit at the end. Already and just sit after have or has. Still sits in front of have not.
8 or more of 10: good, and this outcome is met.
6 or 7: read Card 2 again and do the ones you got wrong.
5 or less: do Card 2 and its practice again first.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1 b, 2 h, 3 a, 4 f, 5 d, 6 c, 7 i, 8 e, 9 j, 10 g
Receipt and reference are the easy two to swap. A receipt comes after you pay; a reference is a number.
9 or 10 right: good. 8 or less: read the four word groups again and do it once more.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. Before I post the document, I make a copy.
2. After the worker stamps the form, I put the receipt in my bag.
3. When the office closes for an hour, I come back in the afternoon.
4. Before I fill in the application, I check the reference.
5. After I read every line, I sign at the end.
6. When the queue is very long, I wait outside.
7. After I make an appointment, I write the date on my hand.
8. After they send me a letter, I collect the new card.
Count your commas. There should be eight, one after each first part.
7 or 8 right: good, and this outcome is met. 6 or less: read Card 3 again and do it twice.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. Four in the afternoon.
2. No. It is closed from one to two.
3. Counter 6.
4. Counter 2.
5. A filled-in and signed form, a document with your name and address, and your reference number.
6. A receipt, with your reference on it.
7. Ten days. After fourteen days, go back with the receipt.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. She has signed the form.
2. I have posted the letter.
3. I have not renewed it yet.
4. Before I leave, I check the list.
5. They sent it yesterday.
6. He has already collected his card.
7. I still have not filled it in.
8. After I sign the form, I put it in the envelope.
1 and 6 are about the word after have or has. 3 and 7 are about where the time word sits.
5 has a day in it, so it takes the past. 4 and 8 want a comma.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: do Cards 1, 2 and 3 again, one a day.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: have — I takes have. Has goes with he, she and it. Am does not go in front of a past form here, and having cannot start this sentence.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: She has signed the form. — She takes has, and after has comes the past form signed. Have is for I, you, we and they. Sign and signing are not past forms.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: collected — After have comes the past form: collected. Collect is the plain verb, collecting is the -ing form, and collects goes with he or she in the present.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: I have not signed it yet. — Yet goes at the end of the sentence. The other three put yet in the middle, where it does not belong in this pattern.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: I have already collected the card. — Already sits between have and the past form collected. The last one also adds yet, and yet cannot go in a finished sentence.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: I still have not got the card. — Still in front of have not means nothing has changed, and it is late. Already and just are for a thing that is done, and the third one names a day.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: just — Just means a very short time ago: I have just come back. Yet is for a thing not done, lately means in the last few weeks, and still means nothing has changed.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Before — Before says when: you check the list first, then you leave. Because gives a reason, but joins two ideas, and between is for place.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: After I sign the form, I post it. — The time part is After I sign the form, so the comma goes at its end. The other three cut the sentence in the wrong place.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: a receipt — A receipt is the small paper you get after you pay. A reference is a short number, an envelope holds a letter, and a signature is your own name.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Cancel it. — To cancel is to stop something that was planned. You collect a thing that is waiting, you renew a card for more time, and you print a paper copy.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: I posted it yesterday. — Yesterday says when, so the sentence takes the past: I posted it. With have, no day is said. Post is not a past form, and yet does not go in a finished sentence.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
